title: What the Accident Left Me Negotiating With
script: Narrator: [measured] There's a particular arrogance native to a body that has never seriously failed you, an unexamined assumption that its cooperation is simply the baseline against which everything else is measured.
Narrator: [reflective] The collision itself lasted perhaps two seconds, and yet it recalibrated, permanently, a set of assumptions I'd carried unchallenged for thirty-four years.
Narrator: [honest] Waking in that hospital bed, I catalogued the damage with a strange, clinical detachment, as though inventorying someone else's misfortune rather than my own.
Narrator: [thoughtful] The detachment, I've since learned, was simply shock wearing the costume of composure, a mercy that expires precisely when you least expect it to.
Narrator: [uneasy] Grief arrived weeks later, once the cast came off and the limp remained, stubborn and undramatic, refusing the tidy resolution recovery narratives generally promise.
Narrator: [honest] I found myself mourning a body I'd never once thanked while it was quietly, competently doing everything I'd asked of it without complaint.
Narrator: [reflective] There's an entire vocabulary of gratitude reserved for health only once it's partially withdrawn, a cruelty in timing I hadn't fully appreciated before.

Narrator: [thoughtful] My physiotherapist, unsentimental in the way I eventually came to value, told me recovery wasn't a return to the previous body but a negotiated settlement with an altogether different one.
Narrator: [analytical] That reframing spared me months of comparing this body unfavourably to a version that, strictly speaking, no longer existed to be compared against.
Narrator: [determined] So I stopped measuring progress against who I'd been, and started measuring it, more modestly, against who I'd been the week before.
Narrator: [warmly] The limp persists on cold mornings, an unglamorous souvenir, though I've stopped experiencing it as an insult and started treating it, oddly, as evidence I survived something.
Narrator: [peacefully] What the accident actually left me negotiating with wasn't my leg, in the end, but a quieter, more permanent humility about what bodies can and cannot promise us.

quiz.question: What arrogance does the narrator describe in the opening?
options: Arrogance about his career achievements
The assumption that a body's cooperation is simply the baseline against which everything else is measured
Arrogance about his intelligence
Pride in his physical strength before the accident
quiz.explanation: He describes the arrogance of assuming a healthy body's cooperation is a baseline rather than something that can fail.

quiz.question: How did the narrator initially react in the hospital bed?
options: With immediate panic and despair
With strange clinical detachment, cataloguing the damage as if it belonged to someone else
With relief that nothing was wrong
With anger at the other driver
quiz.explanation: He describes cataloguing the damage with clinical detachment, as though inventorying someone else's misfortune.

quiz.question: What did the narrator eventually understand that detachment to be?
options: Genuine acceptance
Shock wearing the costume of composure, a mercy that expires unexpectedly
A permanent psychological state
Evidence he wasn't seriously injured
quiz.explanation: He came to understand the detachment was shock disguised as composure, a temporary mercy that eventually expired.

quiz.question: What did the physiotherapist tell him about recovery?
options: That he would fully return to his previous body
That recovery wasn't a return to the previous body but a negotiated settlement with a different one
That recovery was impossible
That he should ignore his limp entirely
quiz.explanation: The physiotherapist reframed recovery as a negotiated settlement with a different body, not a return to the old one.

quiz.question: What does the narrator conclude the accident actually left him negotiating with?
options: His finances
A quieter, more permanent humility about what bodies can and cannot promise
His relationship with his physiotherapist
His career plans
quiz.explanation: He concludes the real negotiation was with a permanent humility about the limits of what a body can promise.

title: Two Friends Debate the Wisdom of Optimizing for a Hundred Years
script: Wisnu: [enthusiastic] I've started fasting on a schedule, tracking my blood markers quarterly, sleeping precisely eight hours. I intend to see a hundred and five, Laras, and I intend to see it well.
Larasati: [amused] That's an admirably specific ambition. Can I ask what you imagine you'll actually be doing with those extra decades?
Wisnu: [defensive] Living them, presumably, with considerably more clarity than most people manage in the decades they've already got.
Larasati: [gentle] I don't doubt the discipline. I question whether longevity, pursued as an end unto itself, quietly displaces the living it was meant to extend.
Wisnu: [challenging] That sounds like the comfortable rationalization of someone who'd rather not confront the discipline required.
Larasati: [wry] Perhaps, though I'd note you've mentioned your blood markers twice already and haven't once mentioned what you actually did yesterday.
Wisnu: [pausing] That's uncomfortably observant. I suppose the tracking has become somewhat consuming, if I'm honest about it.
Larasati: [thoughtful] I'm not arguing against caring for your body. I'm asking whether the vigilance has quietly become the point, rather than remaining a means toward something else entirely.
Wisnu: [honest] I think I'm frightened, underneath the optimization, of an ordinary death arriving before I've actually decided what any of this was for.
Larasati: [understanding] That's a far more interesting confession than the blood markers, and considerably more worth examining.
Wisnu: [reflective] So the tracking is partly a way of postponing that question, deferring meaning by managing metrics instead of actually confronting it.
Larasati: [warmly] That's my suspicion, yes. A hundred and five years spent postponing the question isn't obviously superior to seventy spent having actually answered it.
Wisnu: [considering] I don't think I'm ready to abandon the discipline entirely. But perhaps I'll interrogate why I'm pursuing it quite so anxiously.
Larasati: [encouraging] That seems wiser than either extreme, honestly. Optimize the body, certainly, but don't let the optimizing quietly become the entire life you're optimizing it for.

quiz.question: What has Wisnu started doing to pursue longevity?
options: Taking unproven supplements only
Fasting on a schedule, tracking blood markers quarterly, and sleeping precisely eight hours
Consulting fortune tellers
Avoiding all exercise
quiz.explanation: Wisnu describes fasting on a schedule, quarterly blood marker tracking, and precise sleep as his longevity regimen.

quiz.question: What question does Larasati raise about longevity as a goal?
options: Whether it's medically possible
Whether longevity pursued as an end unto itself quietly displaces the living it was meant to extend
Whether it's too expensive
Whether his doctor approves
quiz.explanation: Larasati questions whether pursuing longevity as an end in itself displaces the actual living it's meant to extend.

quiz.question: What observation does Larasati make about Wisnu's conversation habits?
options: He never discusses health at all
He's mentioned his blood markers twice but hasn't mentioned what he actually did yesterday
He talks only about his job
He avoids discussing the future
quiz.explanation: Larasati points out Wisnu has mentioned blood markers repeatedly but nothing about how he actually spent yesterday.

quiz.question: What fear does Wisnu eventually admit to?
options: Fear of losing his job
Fear of an ordinary death arriving before he's decided what any of this was for
Fear of Larasati's opinion
Fear of failing his blood tests
quiz.explanation: Wisnu admits he fears an ordinary death arriving before he has determined the actual purpose behind his pursuits.

quiz.question: What is Larasati's final suggestion to Wisnu?
options: To abandon all health discipline immediately
To optimize the body but not let optimizing become the entire life being optimized for
To pursue longevity even more aggressively
To stop caring about his health entirely
quiz.explanation: Larasati suggests optimizing the body is fine, but it shouldn't become the entire life being optimized for.

title: Learning the Discipline of Doing Nothing After Surgery
script: Narrator: [wry] Nobody warns you that convalescence demands a discipline entirely its own, one considerably harder to master than whatever discipline got you into the operating theatre in the first place.
Narrator: [reflective] I had assumed, naively, that healing was passive, something the body simply accomplished while I waited it out with mild impatience.

Narrator: [honest] What I discovered instead was an active, almost adversarial relationship with my own restlessness, a mind still operating at full velocity trapped inside a body under strict instruction to idle.
Narrator: [uneasy] The first week, I treated every hour of stillness as time stolen from productivity, an accounting error I was somehow obligated to correct the moment I was cleared to move.

Narrator: [thoughtful] My surgeon, with the weary patience of someone who's delivered this speech many times before, told me healing tissue doesn't negotiate with ambition, however admirable the ambition might otherwise be.
Narrator: [honest] I ignored her, predictably, and reopened something minor that cost me an additional fortnight, a lesson considerably more expensive than simply believing her the first time.

Narrator: [reflective] That setback, humiliating as it felt, taught me something the successful surgery hadn't: that stillness isn't the absence of progress, merely progress operating on a timescale my impatience refused to acknowledge.
Narrator: [thoughtful] I began, slowly, treating the recovery itself as the actual work, rather than an inconvenient interruption to work I'd resume once properly permitted.
Narrator: [analytical] This required unlearning an entire vocabulary I'd absorbed uncritically for years, one that equated worth almost exclusively with visible output and motion.
Narrator: [determined] Lying there, doing observably nothing, I practiced a strange new arithmetic: that healing counted, that rest constituted its own legitimate form of accomplishment.
Narrator: [warmly] Weeks later, fully mended, I noticed something unexpected: the patience convalescence had forced on me hadn't simply evaporated once I was cleared to move again.
Narrator: [peacefully] I still catch myself, occasionally, extending that same reluctant patience toward other areas of life that were never going to be rushed successfully regardless.

quiz.question: What discipline does the narrator say convalescence demands?
options: The same discipline as before surgery
A discipline entirely its own, harder to master than what led her to the operating theatre
No discipline at all
Only physical discipline, not mental
quiz.explanation: She describes convalescence as demanding its own discipline, harder than whatever led her to surgery originally.

quiz.question: What relationship did the narrator discover during the first week?
options: A peaceful, easy acceptance of rest
An active, almost adversarial relationship with her own restlessness
No difficulty adjusting at all
A newfound love of stillness immediately
quiz.explanation: She discovered an adversarial relationship between her restless mind and her body's need to idle.

quiz.question: What happened when the narrator ignored her surgeon's advice?
options: Nothing negative occurred
She reopened something minor, costing an additional fortnight of recovery
She recovered faster than expected
Her surgeon refused to treat her again
quiz.explanation: Ignoring the advice led her to reopen a minor injury, costing an extra two weeks of recovery.

quiz.question: What did the setback teach the narrator that the successful surgery hadn't?
options: That surgery was unnecessary
That stillness isn't the absence of progress, but progress on a different timescale
That doctors are always wrong
That recovery is always instant
quiz.explanation: The setback taught her that stillness is progress operating on a timescale her impatience had refused to acknowledge.

quiz.question: What did the narrator notice weeks later, once fully mended?
options: The patience she developed evaporated instantly
The patience convalescence forced on her hadn't simply evaporated once cleared to move again
She regretted the entire recovery process
She returned to her old habits immediately
quiz.explanation: She noticed the patience she was forced to develop persisted even after she was fully recovered and moving again.

title: A Friend Intervenes on a Caregiver Neglecting Her Own Health
script: Citra: [gentle] Bening, you cancelled your own check-up again, for the third time this year, to take your mother to hers. I need to say something about that pattern.
Bening: [tired] There wasn't really a choice. She needed the ride, and my schedule was the only one flexible enough to accommodate it.
Citra: [firm] There's always technically a choice, even when every option feels equally unacceptable. What I'm worried about is that yours has quietly stopped including you.
Bening: [defensive] I'm fine, Citra. Tired, obviously, but fine in every way that actually matters right now.
Citra: [pointed] You said something nearly identical eight months ago, before the exhaustion turned into that infection you let go untreated for two weeks.
Bening: [uncomfortable] That's not entirely fair. I was busy, not negligent, and those aren't quite the same accusation.
Citra: [gently] I'm not accusing you of negligence toward your mother. I'm suggesting you've become negligent toward yourself, in a way you'd never tolerate from anyone caring for someone you loved.
Bening: [honest] If I'm honest, I don't know how to prioritize myself without it feeling like abandoning her, even briefly, when she needs so much right now.
Citra: [understanding] I think that's the actual belief worth examining, that caring for yourself and caring for her exist in permanent, zero-sum competition.
Bening: [thoughtful] I hadn't articulated it that plainly before, but yes, that's essentially the equation running underneath everything I decide.
Citra: [warmly] What happens to her care, practically, the day your own health finally forces the issue you're currently postponing?
Bening: [uneasy] It collapses considerably worse than a missed check-up ever would, presumably, since there's nobody else positioned to absorb what I currently absorb.
Citra: [encouraging] Then protecting your health isn't selfishness competing against her care. It's the actual precondition for that care continuing at all.
Bening: [reflective] Put that way, postponing my own check-up starts to look less like devotion and more like a risk I've been quietly taking with both of us.
Citra: [warmly] I'll drive her next time, and you'll go to your own appointment that same afternoon. No further negotiation on this particular point.

quiz.question: What pattern does Citra confront Bening about?
options: Bening missing work deadlines
Bening cancelling her own check-ups repeatedly to take her mother to appointments
Bening avoiding her mother entirely
Bening spending too much money on healthcare
quiz.explanation: Citra confronts Bening about cancelling her own medical check-ups multiple times to prioritize her mother's care.

quiz.question: What happened eight months ago that Citra references?
options: Bening got a promotion
Exhaustion turned into an infection Bening let go untreated for two weeks
Bening's mother recovered fully
Nothing significant happened
quiz.explanation: Citra references how Bening's earlier exhaustion led to an untreated infection lasting two weeks.

quiz.question: What belief does Bening admit underlies her decisions?
options: That her mother doesn't need her help
That caring for herself and caring for her mother exist in permanent, zero-sum competition
That she has unlimited time and energy
That her own health doesn't matter to anyone
quiz.explanation: Bening admits she believes self-care and caring for her mother compete in a zero-sum way, so one must lose.

quiz.question: What does Citra ask Bening to consider about her mother's care long-term?
options: Whether her mother would approve
What happens to her mother's care the day Bening's own health finally forces the issue
Whether her mother has other family members
Whether the appointments are truly necessary
quiz.explanation: Citra asks what happens to the caregiving arrangement when Bening's neglected health eventually forces a crisis.

quiz.question: How does Citra reframe protecting Bening's own health?
options: As selfishness that competes with caring for her mother
As the actual precondition for that care continuing at all
As entirely unrelated to her mother's wellbeing
As something Bening should feel guilty about
quiz.explanation: Citra reframes self-care not as competing selfishness but as the precondition that allows the caregiving to continue.

title: Voice Memo While Tapering Off Medication I've Taken for Years
script: Narrator: [uncertain] Recording this on week three of tapering, mostly to have some honest account of a process everyone around me insists on narrating as unambiguously triumphant.
Narrator: [honest] It doesn't feel triumphant, particularly. It feels like slowly removing scaffolding from a structure nobody's entirely certain can stand unassisted yet.
Narrator: [reflective] Eight years on this medication, long enough that I've genuinely forgotten which version of my temperament belongs to the drug and which belongs, more fundamentally, to me.
Narrator: [thoughtful] That's the part nobody adequately prepares you for, the unsettling ambiguity of not knowing where the treatment ends and the actual self quietly resumes.
Narrator: [uneasy] Friends keep asking whether I feel more like myself now, a question I find myself unable to answer honestly, since I no longer possess a reliable baseline to compare against.

Narrator: [wry] There's an irony here I can't quite escape: the medication that once rescued me from a version of myself I couldn't tolerate has become, itself, a version I'm now cautiously testing whether I can tolerate leaving.
Narrator: [honest] My psychiatrist has been admirably unhurried about this, refusing to frame it as either victory or defeat, merely as information we're gathering carefully, together.
Narrator: [thoughtful] She reminded me that tapering successfully doesn't retroactively mean the medication was unnecessary, a reframe I've had to return to more than once already this week.
Narrator: [reflective] Some days the anxiety resurfaces with a familiarity that frightens me, an old visitor I'd assumed had permanently relocated elsewhere.
Narrator: [determined] Other days pass almost unremarkably, which itself feels like a small, quiet victory I'm learning not to over-interpret in either direction.
Narrator: [warmly] I've stopped asking whether I'll eventually be entirely medication-free, and started asking, instead, whether whatever configuration I land on actually lets me live well.
Narrator: [peacefully] That's a considerably more modest question than the one I started with, and, I'm slowly discovering, a considerably more honest one too.

quiz.question: What is the narrator doing at the time of this recording?
options: Starting a new medication
Tapering off a medication he's taken for eight years
Recovering from surgery
Preparing for a doctor's appointment
quiz.explanation: He is in week three of tapering off medication he has taken for eight years.

quiz.question: How does the narrator describe the tapering process, contrary to how others narrate it?
options: As unambiguously triumphant
Like slowly removing scaffolding from a structure nobody's certain can stand unassisted yet
As completely painless
As something he regrets starting
quiz.explanation: He describes it not as triumphant but as scaffolding removal from an uncertain structure, contrary to others' framing.

quiz.question: What ambiguity does the narrator say nobody adequately prepares you for?
options: The cost of medication
Not knowing where the treatment ends and the actual self resumes
How long the taper will take
Whether doctors will approve
quiz.explanation: He struggles with the ambiguity of distinguishing which parts of his temperament belong to the drug versus himself.

quiz.question: What did his psychiatrist remind him about tapering successfully?
options: That it proves the medication was never needed
That it doesn't retroactively mean the medication was unnecessary
That it means he is fully cured
That it should happen faster
quiz.explanation: His psychiatrist reminded him that a successful taper doesn't mean the medication was unnecessary in the first place.

quiz.question: What question does the narrator say he has replaced his original question with?
options: Whether he will ever be entirely medication-free
Whether whatever configuration he lands on actually lets him live well
Whether his friends approve of the decision
Whether the medication was ever effective
quiz.explanation: He has replaced the question of being medication-free with the more modest question of whether he can live well.

title: A Doctor Helps a Patient Sit With an Incurable Diagnosis
script: Yulia: [numb] So when you say manageable rather than curable, I need you to be precise. What exactly am I supposed to do with that distinction?
Dr. Hakim: [gentle] It means the disease likely won't disappear, but it also, in most cases like yours, doesn't dictate the length or shape of your life as severely as you might currently fear.
Yulia: [frustrated] That's a strangely comforting sentence wrapped around a genuinely devastating fact. I'm not sure which half I'm supposed to hold onto.
Dr. Hakim: [honest] Both, probably, uncomfortably, at the same time. Most of my patients eventually learn to hold contradictory truths without needing to resolve them into something simpler.
Yulia: [uncertain] I keep waiting for the moment this becomes real to me, and instead I just feel oddly suspended, like I'm hearing about someone else's diagnosis.
Dr. Hakim: [understanding] That suspension is common, and not something to rush past. Denial, in measured doses, is occasionally a reasonable pace for absorbing something this large.
Yulia: [honest] My mother wants me to fight it, loudly, publicly, the way people talk about illness in inspirational posters.

Dr. Hakim: [thoughtful] Militaristic language helps some people genuinely. For others, it quietly implies that those who don't recover simply didn't fight hard enough, which is neither accurate nor kind.
Yulia: [relieved] Thank you for saying that. I've felt vaguely guilty for not wanting to narrate this as a battle.
Dr. Hakim: [warmly] You're permitted whatever narrative actually helps you function, provided it doesn't quietly become a performance for everyone else's comfort instead of yours.
Yulia: [reflective] What does managing this well actually look like, practically?
Dr. Hakim: [practical] Honestly, ordinary life, adjusted rather than abandoned, without being entirely organized around it.
Yulia: [thoughtful] That sounds almost anticlimactic compared to what I imagined this conversation would feel like.
Dr. Hakim: [warmly] Most durable coping is anticlimactic, in my experience. The dramatic version rarely sustains itself past the first few difficult months.
Yulia: [determined] Then I suppose I'll aim for anticlimactic. It sounds, oddly, like the more honest kind of courage available to me right now.
Dr. Hakim: [sincere] I think it is. And I'll be here for the unglamorous, ordinary parts of managing this, for as long as you need.

quiz.question: What distinction does Yulia ask Dr. Hakim to clarify?
options: The difference between two medications
The difference between manageable and curable
The cost of treatment
The length of hospital stays
quiz.explanation: Yulia asks Dr. Hakim to precisely explain the difference between describing her condition as manageable rather than curable.

quiz.question: How does Dr. Hakim describe most patients' eventual relationship with contradictory truths?
options: They must resolve them into something simpler immediately
They eventually learn to hold contradictory truths without needing to resolve them
They avoid thinking about the diagnosis entirely
They always choose denial permanently
quiz.explanation: Dr. Hakim explains most patients learn to hold contradictory truths simultaneously without forcing resolution.

quiz.question: What concern does Dr. Hakim raise about militaristic 'fighting' language?
options: It is always the most helpful framing
It can quietly imply that those who don't recover simply didn't fight hard enough
It has no effect on patients either way
It is required by medical guidelines
quiz.explanation: Dr. Hakim notes militaristic language can imply that non-recovery reflects insufficient effort, which is neither accurate nor kind.

quiz.question: What does Dr. Hakim say managing the illness well actually looks like?
options: A dramatic, constant battle
Ordinary life, adjusted rather than abandoned, organized around the illness only partially
Complete isolation from daily responsibilities
Ignoring the diagnosis entirely
quiz.explanation: He describes managing well as building an adjusted version of ordinary life rather than one entirely organized around illness.

quiz.question: How does Dr. Hakim describe most durable coping?
options: As dramatic and inspiring
As anticlimactic, since dramatic coping rarely sustains itself past the first difficult months
As something only a few patients achieve
As identical to denial
quiz.explanation: Dr. Hakim says durable coping is usually anticlimactic, since the dramatic version rarely lasts beyond initial difficult months.

title: A Podcast on the Athlete Who Couldn't Stop Training
script: Host: [warmly] Today's guest is a sports physiotherapist who works primarily with athletes struggling not with injury exactly, but with an inability to stop training even when injured. Welcome, Coach Ridwan.
Coach Ridwan: [pleasant] Thank you. It's an underdiscussed problem, largely because it masquerades so convincingly as admirable discipline.
Host: [curious] Talk us through what overtraining actually looks like when it crosses into something closer to compulsion.
Coach Ridwan: [explaining] The clearest marker is a rest day producing genuine anxiety rather than relief, as though stillness itself were the injury requiring treatment.
Host: [interested] So the athlete has essentially inverted the relationship, fearing recovery more than fearing the damage that skipping it actually causes.
Coach Ridwan: [nodding] Precisely, and it's rarely about vanity or ambition alone. Frequently, performance has become the only domain where the athlete feels their worth is legible to themselves.
Host: [thoughtful] That's a heavier explanation than I expected for what sounds, superficially, like excessive gym attendance.

Coach Ridwan: [serious] It usually is heavier. I've worked with athletes who could articulate, precisely, the biomechanics of their injury while remaining entirely unable to articulate why stopping felt unbearable.
Host: [curious] How do you actually intervene, given that the behaviour presents as virtue rather than as the problem it actually is?
Coach Ridwan: [thoughtful] Slowly, and rarely through direct confrontation. I start by asking what they imagine they'd lose, specifically, if performance stopped being the metric defining them.
Host: [interested] And what do they typically answer?
Coach Ridwan: [reflective] Often nothing coherent at first, which is itself revealing. The identity has been so thoroughly fused with output that the question genuinely stumps them.
Host: [curious] Is there a recovery story you'd point to that illustrates the shift actually happening?

Coach Ridwan: [warmly] One athlete, after a forced six-month break from a stress fracture, told me she'd rediscovered interests she hadn't touched since adolescence, simply because training no longer consumed every available hour.
Host: [interested] So the injury, paradoxically, became the intervention the discipline itself never would have permitted.
Coach Ridwan: [wry] Exactly that irony. Sometimes the body forces the rest that judgment alone was never going to grant it voluntarily.
Host: [smiling] A genuinely illuminating conversation. Thank you, Coach Ridwan.
Coach Ridwan: [warmly] My pleasure. Now, if you'll excuse me, I have my own rest day to reluctantly honour.

quiz.question: What problem does Coach Ridwan work with athletes on?
options: Recovering from broken bones only
An inability to stop training even when injured, which masquerades as discipline
Choosing the right diet
Finding sponsorships
quiz.explanation: Coach Ridwan works with athletes who cannot stop training even when injured, a compulsion disguised as admirable discipline.

quiz.question: What is the clearest marker of overtraining crossing into compulsion?
options: Improved performance metrics
A rest day producing genuine anxiety rather than relief
Increased appetite
Better sleep quality
quiz.explanation: He identifies the clearest marker as anxiety, rather than relief, arising from a scheduled rest day.

quiz.question: What does Coach Ridwan say performance often becomes for these athletes?
options: An enjoyable hobby only
The only domain where the athlete feels their worth is legible to themselves
A financial necessity exclusively
Something they don't care about at all
quiz.explanation: He explains performance often becomes the only domain where these athletes feel their self-worth is legible.

quiz.question: How does Coach Ridwan typically begin intervening?
options: Through direct confrontation immediately
By asking what they imagine they'd lose if performance stopped defining them
By banning them from all training instantly
By ignoring the issue entirely
quiz.explanation: He starts slowly by asking what the athlete imagines losing if performance stopped being their defining metric.

quiz.question: What happened to the athlete after her forced six-month break?
options: She quit sports entirely and regretted it
She rediscovered interests from adolescence since training no longer consumed every hour
She returned immediately to overtraining
Nothing changed for her at all
quiz.explanation: The athlete rediscovered old interests during her forced break, since training no longer occupied all her available time.
